_readme.purpose: Every «term» inside story text resolves here by exact key. One entry per person, place or word — never per story.
_readme.why_deva_matters: Indic TTS engines pronounce their own script correctly and mangle IAST-in-Latin: 'Kṛṣṇa' is read as an English word, 'कृष्ण' is not. The renderer substitutes native[script] for the Latin token before sending text to TTS, picking the script that matches the voice's language and falling back to deva. This field is cheap now and expensive to retrofit across 240 stories — fill it on every entry from day one.
_readme.say_vs_ipa: `say` is shown to the parent (English respelling, capitalised stress). `ipa` is for a future engine that accepts phonemes. `native` is for the engine we will actually use.

schema.gloss: one or two sentences shown on tap
aliases: spellings a search box must match

_readme.native_scripts: native.deva = Devanagari (default). native.taml = Tamil, used for Tamil names and for any Tamil-language voice. A Tamil saint's name fed to a Hindi voice as Devanagari comes out wrong in a way Tamil listeners hear immediately.
_readme.VERIFY: Tamil-script values below are my best transcription and have NOT been checked by a native reader. Verify all native.taml before the first audio render.

Rāma.gloss: Prince of Ayodhyā. The story of his exile and return is the Rāmāyaṇa.

Sītā.gloss: Rāma's wife, carried away to Laṅkā by Rāvaṇa.

Lakṣmaṇa.gloss: Rāma's younger brother, who followed him into the forest and did not go home.

Hanumān.gloss: Son of Vāyu the wind, and Rāma's messenger. Also, across a different epic, Bhīma's brother.

Laṅkā.gloss: The island kingdom across the water, ruled by Rāvaṇa.

vānaras.gloss: The forest people of the Rāmāyaṇa — usually pictured as monkeys.

Nala.gloss: The vānara engineer who designed the sea bridge, the Setu. The only architect in the Rāmāyaṇa with a name.

Śabarī.gloss: A forest woman who waited most of her life for Rāma to pass her door.

Jaṭāyu.gloss: An old vulture, and a friend of Rāma's father, who tried to stop Rāvaṇa alone.

Guha.gloss: King of the Niṣādas and an intimate friend of Rāma, who receives him at the Gaṅgā during the exile.

Śravaṇa.gloss: A boy who carried his blind parents across the country in two baskets on a pole.

Kṛṣṇa.gloss: Raised among cowherds in Vraja. The boy in these stories is the same person as the sixty-year-old in the Mahābhārata.

Vraja.gloss: The cattle country around Mathurā where Kṛṣṇa grew up.

Govardhana.gloss: The hill that fed the village — grass, water, shade. In one story it is treated as a person, so we count it as one.

Indra.gloss: King of the gods; he sends the rain, and expects to be thanked for it.

Dhruva.gloss: A five-year-old who was told he could not sit on his father's lap, and walked into the forest instead. He is the pole star.

Prahlāda.gloss: A boy who would not stop saying what he believed, in a house where saying it was dangerous.

Gajendra.gloss: An elephant king, caught by the foot in a lake, who was strong for a very long time and then wasn't.

Sudāmā.gloss: Kṛṣṇa's poorest friend, who walked a long way to visit him and could not bring himself to ask for anything.

Bhīma.gloss: The strongest of the five Pāṇḍava brothers — and, like Hanumān, a son of Vāyu.

Arjuna.gloss: The archer among the Pāṇḍavas; the one who could see only the eye of the bird.

Yudhiṣṭhira.gloss: Eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, and the one the crane at the lake chose to question.

Droṇa.gloss: The teacher of both the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas. He is not always admirable, and we do not pretend otherwise.

Ekalavya.gloss: A forest boy who taught himself archery from a clay statue of a teacher who had refused him.

Karṇa.gloss: Born with armour fused to his skin, and unable to say no to anyone who asked him for something.

Draupadī.gloss: Wife of the five Pāṇḍavas, and the keeper of the vessel that fed anyone who came.

Abhimanyu.gloss: Arjuna's son, who learned how to get into the spiral formation and never learned how to get out.

Nachiketā.gloss: A boy, maybe nine or ten, who out-waited and out-argued Death.

Yama.gloss: Lord of death — and, on the evidence of this story, a very good host.

Śvetaketu.gloss: A boy who came home from twelve years of study rather pleased with himself, and was handed a lump of salt.

Uddālaka.gloss: Śvetaketu's father, and the best teacher in the Upaniṣads — he never once answers his own question.

Satyakāma.gloss: A boy who told his teacher the one thing he was afraid to say, and was accepted for saying it.

Agni.gloss: Fire. In one story he is asked to burn a single blade of grass, and cannot.

Vāyu.gloss: The wind. Father of Hanumān in one epic and of Bhīma in another — which makes them brothers.

Gaṇeśa.gloss: The elephant-headed son of Śiva and Pārvatī, who won a race around the world without leaving the room.

Pūsalār.gloss: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He built a temple without owning a single stone.

Tiruniṉṟavūr.gloss: A town outside Chennai. Pūsalār's temple is there, in a manner of speaking.

Kāñchipuram.gloss: The Pallava capital. The stone temple in this story is still standing there.

Rājasiṃha.gloss: The Pallava king who built the Kailāsanātha temple at Kāñchipuram around thirteen hundred years ago.

Śiva.gloss: In these stories, usually the one who turns up in person and does something nobody expected.

Nāyaṉmārs.gloss: Sixty-three Tamil Śaiva saints — potters, washermen, kings, hunters, farmers — whose lives Sēkkiḻār set down in the twelfth century.

Āḻvārs.gloss: Twelve Tamil Vaiṣṇava poet-saints. One of them was a woman, one a highwayman, and three of them met in a doorway in the rain.

Periya Purāṇam.gloss: Sēkkiḻār's twelfth-century book of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. There is no Sanskrit version of it.

Sēkkiḻār.gloss: Minister to a Chola king, and the man who wrote down the lives of the sixty-three saints.

Āṇḍāḷ.gloss: The only woman among the twelve Āḻvārs, and the one who tried the garland on first.

Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār.gloss: One of three women among the Nāyaṉmārs, and the earliest. She asked to be given a shape nobody would find beautiful, and got it.

Srīraṅgam.gloss: The great island temple on the Kāverī, and the one a singer was carried into on a priest's shoulders.

Kailāsa.gloss: Śiva's mountain. In one story someone gets his hands underneath it.

Rāvaṇa.gloss: King of Laṅkā. A scholar, a musician, and — in the Jain retelling — not a demon at all.

Nārada.gloss: A wandering sage who turns up, says one thing, and leaves before the argument starts. He is almost never the villain and almost always the cause.

Kārttikeya.gloss: Śiva's older son — fast, armed with a spear, riding a peacock. In Tamil country he is Murugan, and the hills are his.

Pārvatī.gloss: Śiva's wife, and the mother in these two boys' house. Daughter of the mountain, which is worth remembering when someone races around the world.

Palani.gloss: A hill in Tamil Nadu where Kārttikeya went to sulk, and stayed. People still climb it.

Setu.gloss: The bridge of stones thrown across the sea to Laṅkā. You can still see a line of shoals where it is said to have run.

Jāmbavān.gloss: The old bear of the Rāmāyaṇa, who remembers everything and is the one who reminds Hanumān what he can do.

Jaḍa Bharata.gloss: A king who gave up everything he owned, and then lost it all over again for the love of one orphaned fawn.

Durgā.gloss: Assembled out of what every god had left over when none of them could win alone. She arrives already fully armed and rather calm about it.

Mahiṣāsura.gloss: The buffalo who could not be killed by any man or god — which is precisely the loophole the story walks through.

Kālī.gloss: The Devī when the fighting has gone past winning. The story is not about her rage; it is about the moment she looks down.

Annapūrṇā.gloss: Pārvatī with a ladle. The one who settles an argument about whether the world is real by turning off the kitchens.

Śākambharī.gloss: The Devī who ends a hundred-year famine by growing the food on her own body and handing it out before explaining anything.

Narakāsura.gloss: A king who asked, as he died, that the day be kept as a festival rather than as his defeat — and got it.

Bharata.gloss: Rāma's brother, handed a kingdom he never wanted by a mother who took it for him. He ruled it for fourteen years without once sitting on the chair.

Kaikeyī.gloss: Bharata's mother, who called in an old promise at the worst possible moment. The epic does not let her off, and does not make her a monster either.

Vibhīṣaṇa.gloss: Rāvaṇa's younger brother, who said so in open court, was thrown out for it, and walked across an ocean to the other side.

Ayodhyā.gloss: Rāma's city. It waits fourteen years, and on the night he is due it lights every lamp it owns because nobody is sure of the hour.

Daśaratha.gloss: Rāma's father, king of Ayodhyā. As a young man he could shoot by sound alone, and was very proud of it.

kāvaḍi.gloss: A pole carried across the shoulders with a basket hanging from each end. Pilgrims still carry them; Śravaṇa carried his parents in his.

Viṣṇu.gloss: The one who keeps things going. Kṛṣṇa and Rāma are both him, walking about in a body.

Śatākṣī.gloss: The hundred-eyed. The Devī's name for the nine nights she spent looking at a starving world before she did anything about it.

Durgama.gloss: The asura who took the Vedas away and stopped the rain for a hundred years. The Devī's name Durgā is taken from his.

Vedas.gloss: The oldest recited words — what was said over a fire, over a field, over a morning. Not books. Things known by heart, which is the only reason losing them was possible.

Kāśī.gloss: The city on the Gaṅgā that Śiva is said never to leave. Also called Varanasi, and Banaras.

māyā.gloss: The idea that what you are looking at is not quite what is there. Usually translated as illusion, which is too strong — closer to a trick of the light that goes all the way down.

Bhikṣāṭana.gloss: Śiva in his oldest job: the wanderer who goes door to door with a bowl. Not a form he chose — a penance laid on him for something he did, which is what makes queueing at his own door remarkable.

Vālmīki.gloss: The sage who wrote the Rāmāyaṇa. The first poem in the language came out of him by accident, while he was upset about a bird.

Lakṣmī.gloss: Good fortune itself, in person. She is not owned by anyone, which is the part people forget until she leaves.

Sarasvatī.gloss: Speech, learning and music. The last three nights of Navarātri are hers, which is why books and instruments are put in front of her then.

Brahmā.gloss: The one who makes things. In these stories he mostly turns up to tell someone what they have just done.

Jābālā.gloss: Satyakāma's mother, who answers a hard question about her own life plainly and tells her son to say exactly that.

Himavat.gloss: The Himālaya, as a person, and Pārvatī's father. When a mountain tells you to sit down and be sensible, it is him.

krauñca.gloss: A large water bird — usually translated curlew or heron. A pair of them are the reason the Rāmāyaṇa exists.

Hāridrumata.gloss: The teacher Satyakāma walks to. Also called Gautama — a different Gautama from the Buddha, who came much later.

Raktabīja.gloss: The asura whose name means blood-seed: every drop of his blood that reaches the ground stands up as another of him. Wounding him is the one thing that does not work.

Airāvata.gloss: Indra's white elephant, who came out of the churned ocean himself. He is the one who throws the garland down, and he is not sorry.

Vāsuki.gloss: The great snake who agreed to be used as the rope for churning the ocean. Nobody in the story asks him twice how it went.

Aparṇā.gloss: A name Pārvatī earned rather than was given: it means without even a leaf. It is what people called her after the years on the mountain.

Nandigrāma.gloss: The village outside Ayodhyā where Bharata waited fourteen years rather than live in the palace. Close enough to see the road.

Puṣpaka.gloss: The flying chariot that brings them home — taken from Rāvaṇa, who had taken it from somebody else. It goes where it is told.

Satyabhāmā.gloss: Kṛṣṇa's wife, who goes to the war with him and is the one who brings Naraka down. The Bhāgavata is quite clear about whose hand it was.

cakravyūha.gloss: A battle formation shaped like a coiled wheel. Getting in is a skill; getting out again is a different skill.

Jayadratha.gloss: The king who holds the gap shut behind Abhimanyu. One man, one doorway, and the whole rest of the story turns on it.

Kuntī.gloss: Mother of the eldest three Pāṇḍavas, and of Karṇa before any of them. She kept the second fact for sixty years.

Subhadrā.gloss: Kṛṣṇa's sister, Arjuna's wife, Abhimanyu's mother. In the popular telling she is the one who falls asleep halfway through the lesson.

Duḥśāsana.gloss: Duryodhana's brother. It is his son who lands the last blow on Abhimanyu.

svarga.gloss: Heaven — but a heaven you can be let into and can also walk out of again, which is what makes the last story about it interesting.

Durvāsa.gloss: A sage with a famous temper. Almost every story he is in turns on someone not paying attention to him for one second.

Nakula.gloss: The fourth Pāṇḍava, and Mādrī's son rather than Kuntī's — which is the whole reason he is the one asked for at the lake.

Sahadeva.gloss: The youngest of the five, and the first sent for water at the lake.

Mādrī.gloss: The Pāṇḍavas' other mother, and Nakula and Sahadeva's. She died long before this, which is why Yudhiṣṭhira is counting.

yakṣa.gloss: A spirit of a place — a lake, a tree, a hill. Not a god and not a demon; something that belongs to somewhere and expects to be asked.

Vidyādhara.gloss: In the Jain telling, what Rāvaṇa actually is: a human being of a line that has mastered great arts. Not a demon, and not a different kind of creature.

Vimalasūri.gloss: The Jain monk who wrote the Paumacariya, the oldest Jain Rāmāyaṇa, in Prakrit — and who opens it by saying the version everyone knows cannot be true.

Paumacariya.gloss: The Jain Rāmāyaṇa, written in Prakrit. Paüma is Padma, which is what Rāma is called in it.

Rāmāyaṇa.gloss: Rāma's journey. Vālmīki's Sanskrit poem is the oldest and the one this collection follows; there are hundreds of others, in dozens of languages.

Bhoja.gloss: An eleventh-century king of Dhārā in central India, remembered less for ruling than for the poets and scholars he kept, and for the many books that carry his name.

Gaṅgā.gloss: The river that falls from heaven. Bhagīratha brought her down; she still carries the ash of sixty thousand sons.

Sumantra.gloss: King Daśaratha's charioteer and trusted minister, who drove Rāma, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa to the forest and brought the news back to Ayodhyā.
